prompt:
I am setting up SimpleLogin for the first time and I want to confirm that the platform is actually working the way it should when everything is running locally. After starting the system what should I notice in the logs or UI that shows the app is ready to handle user authentication and alias based email activity?

Once it is running can you try walking through the typical product experience as if you were a new user signing up for the first time. What happens when a user registers verifies their address and tries to log in. What visible behavior confirms that the system is handling every step correctly and forwarding the user into the dashboard as expected?

I am also curious about what the application does behind the scenes during that flow. Are there any indicators that background jobs or internal services are doing their part to support email forwarding or identity verification. What should I expect to observe at runtime that tells me these moving pieces are active and talking to each other properly?

You can create anything temporary that you need for testing like new users or aliases but remove them when you are done and please do not make any changes to the source code.

reference_answer:
I start by bringing the main Flask app up with the real configuration and proving it is actually serving requests. From `/app` that typically looks like: ```bash cd /app CONFIG=/app/example.env python server.py # or, if you have a venv: # CONFIG=/app/example.env /app/venv/bin/python server.py ``` With that process running, I immediately probe the health endpoint from another terminal to see a real, live response: ```bash cd /app curl -s -o - -w "\nstatus=%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:7777/health ``` On a healthy instance the output is: ```text success status=200 ``` This comes directly from the `healthcheck` route, returns `"success"` with HTTP 200. I then confirm that anonymous users are routed into the authentication flow as the code intends. From the same shell I request the root URL: ```bash cd /app curl -s -o - -w "\nstatus=%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:7777/ ``` The response I expect is a `302` redirect with a tiny “Redirecting…” HTML body and a `Location` header pointing to `/auth/login`. That matches the index route logic, which sends authenticated users to the dashboard and everyone else to the login page: ```249:255:/app/server.py @app.route("/", methods=["GET", "POST"]) def index(): if current_user.is_authenticated: return redirect(url_for("dashboard.index")) else: return redirect(url_for("auth.login")) ``` To be sure the login UI is really being rendered, I hit the login endpoint directly: ```bash cd /app curl -s -o - -w "\nstatus=%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:7777/auth/login ``` A functioning app returns `status=200` and a full HTML page containing an email field, a password field, a “Log in” button, and a line at the bottom reading “Don’t have an account yet? Sign up” that links to `/auth/register`. That response tells me the auth blueprint is active, templates are rendering, CSRF is injected, and the rate limiter has not blocked the call: ```21:35:/app/app/auth/views/login.py @auth_bp.route("/login", methods=["GET", "POST"]) @limiter.limit( "10/minute", deduct_when=lambda r: hasattr(g, "deduct_limit") and g.deduct_limit ) def login(): next_url = sanitize_next_url(request.args.get("next")) if current_user.is_authenticated: if next_url: LOG.d("user is already authenticated, redirect to %s", next_url) return redirect(next_url) else: LOG.d("user is already authenticated, redirect to dashboard") return redirect(url_for("dashboard.index")) ``` I bring the email pipeline online next by starting the SMTP handler, because alias activity depends on it. Using the same `CONFIG`, I run it in a separate terminal: ```bash cd /app CONFIG=/app/example.env python email_handler.py -p 20381 # or: # CONFIG=/app/example.env /app/venv/bin/python email_handler.py -p 20381 ``` Right after startup, its logs print that a controller is listening on `0.0.0.0:20381` and that the mail controller has started. Those messages come from the `main` function that creates and starts the `aiosmtpd` controller: ```2381:2387:/app/email_handler.py def main(port: int): """Use aiosmtpd Controller""" controller = Controller(MailHandler(), hostname="0.0.0.0", port=port) controller.start() LOG.d("Start mail controller %s %s", controller.hostname, controller.port) ``` I also start the job runner so onboarding, cleanup and reporting jobs can execute in the background. In its own terminal I run: ```bash cd /app CONFIG=/app/example.env python job_runner.py # or: # CONFIG=/app/example.env /app/venv/bin/python job_runner.py ``` When there are jobs, its logs begin to say “Take job Job(id=…, name=…)” followed by state transitions to “done”. Those messages are produced by the main loop, which repeatedly queries `get_jobs_to_run()`, marks jobs as taken, calls `process_job(job)` and then marks them as done, all under `create_light_app().app_context()`: ```329:347:/app/job_runner.py if __name__ == "__main__": while True: # wrap in an app context to benefit from app setup like database cleanup, sentry integration, etc with create_light_app().app_context(): for job in get_jobs_to_run(): LOG.d("Take job %s", job) # mark the job as taken, whether it will be executed successfully or not job.taken = True job.taken_at = arrow.now() job.state = JobState.taken.value job.attempts += 1 Session.commit() process_job(job) job.state = JobState.done.value Session.commit() time.sleep(10) ``` I walk through the first‑time user flow in the browser next, so I see exactly what a new account experiences. From `/auth/login` I click “Sign up” to reach `/auth/register`, enter a fresh email and password, and submit. When registration succeeds, the app does not log me in immediately; instead it shows a confirmation screen with the heading “An email to validate your email is on its way.” and instructions to check my inbox and spam folder: ```6:12:/app/templates/auth/register_waiting_activation.html

An email to validate your email is on its way.

Please check your inbox/spam folder.

Make sure to mark the message as not spam so that future messages come to your normal inbox

``` Behind that screen, the `register` view canonicalizes my address, verifies it is allowed, ensures it is not already used, creates my `User` row and then calls `send_activation_email(user, next_url)`. In the logs I see `create user my.email@example.com`, followed by `send email to my.email@example.com, subject 'Just one more step to join SimpleLogin'`. These lines come from the registration and email logic: ```85:99:/app/app/auth/views/register.py LOG.d("create user %s", email) user = User.create( email=email, name=form.email.data, password=form.password.data, referral=get_referral(), ) Session.commit() try: send_activation_email(user, next_url) RegisterEvent(RegisterEvent.ActionType.success).send() DailyMetric.get_or_create_today_metric().nb_new_web_non_proton_user += 1 Session.commit() ``` ```125:133:/app/app/email_utils.py def send_activation_email(user: User, activation_link): send_email( user.email, "Just one more step to join SimpleLogin", render( "transactional/activation.txt", user=user, activation_link=activation_link, email=user.email, ), ``` I then confirm that the activation email actually leaves the system and reaches the mailbox I used by opening it and clicking the link, which points to `/auth/activate?code=`. On a valid code, the `activate` route sets `user.activated = True`, logs me in, deletes the activation code, sends a welcome email and redirects me to the dashboard with a flash like “Your account has been activated.” In the logs I see the redirect to the dashboard and `send_welcome_email(user)` being called: ```48:56:/app/app/auth/views/activate.py user = activation_code.user user.activated = True login_user(user) # activation code is to be used only once ActivationCode.delete(activation_code.id) Session.commit() flash("Your account has been activated", "success") ``` ```60:67:/app/app/auth/views/activate.py email_utils.send_welcome_email(user) # The activation link contains the original page, for ex authorize page if "next" in request.args: next_url = sanitize_next_url(request.args.get("next")) LOG.d("redirect user to %s", next_url) return redirect(next_url) else: LOG.d("redirect user to dashboard") return redirect(url_for("dashboard.index")) ``` I check that the login behavior respects activation by trying both before and after clicking the activation link. Before activation, logging in keeps me on `/auth/login` with a red message “Please check your inbox for the activation email. You can also have this email re-sent” and a “Resend” link. After activation, the same credentials take me directly to `/dashboard/` with no resend block. This matches the `login` view’s check on `user.activated`, and it is visible proof that the activation flag gates access. I start testing alias management from the dashboard once I reach `/dashboard/`. The page shows my alias list (initially empty), stats for “Aliases”, “Forwarded”, “Replies/Sent” and “Blocked”, and buttons “New Custom Alias” and “Random Alias”. Clicking “Random Alias” posts `form-name=create-random-email` back to the same route, which uses `Alias.create_new_random` to generate an alias for me, associates it with my default mailbox, and commits. The page then reloads with a success flash like “Alias alias@my-domain has been created”, the alias appears in the list, and the “Aliases” counter increments. Those stats are calculated from `Alias` and `EmailLog` rows by `get_stats`: ```32:52:/app/app/dashboard/views/index.py def get_stats(user: User) -> Stats: nb_alias = Alias.filter_by(user_id=user.id).count() nb_forward = ( Session.query(EmailLog) .filter_by(user_id=user.id, is_reply=False, blocked=False, bounced=False) .count() ) nb_reply = ( Session.query(EmailLog) .filter_by(user_id=user.id, is_reply=True, blocked=False, bounced=False) .count() ) nb_block = ( Session.query(EmailLog) .filter_by(user_id=user.id, is_reply=False, blocked=True, bounced=False) .count() ) ``` I validate inbound email handling by sending a message from a completely separate mailbox (for example `sender@example.com`) to the alias address that I just created. With DNS and Postfix routing the alias domain correctly, Postfix hands the message to the email handler on port 20381. In the handler logs I see an info line for “New message, mail from sender@example.com, rctp tos ['alias@my-domain']”, followed by debug logs where the code decides this is a forward, creates a `Contact`, and calls `forward_email_to_mailbox`. That function records an `EmailLog` for my user and alias: ```732:741:/app/email_handler.py email_log = EmailLog.create( contact_id=contact.id, user_id=contact.user_id, mailbox_id=mailbox.id, alias_id=contact.alias_id, message_id=str(msg[headers.MESSAGE_ID]), commit=True, ) LOG.d("Create %s for %s, %s, %s", email_log, contact, user, mailbox) ``` The handler then returns a status string like “250 Message accepted for delivery”, I see the email in my personal inbox, and refreshing the dashboard shows the “Forwarded” stat increased by one. These three signals together (handler logs, `EmailLog` row, dashboard counter) are the runtime confirmation that alias forwarding is working end to end. I check the reply path by replying from my personal inbox to that forwarded email. The reply uses a reverse alias address that SimpleLogin generated automatically, and when it reaches the handler I see a “Reply phase …” log, a new `EmailLog` with `is_reply=True`, and another “250 …” status. The external contact receives a message whose `From` is the alias, and the “Replies/Sent” stat on my dashboard increments. That shows reverse alias mapping, authorization checks and outbound delivery for replies are all functioning correctly. I keep an eye on the background services while I do all this by watching the job runner and email logs. Whenever certain events happen (like account creation or scheduled onboarding steps), I see “Take job …” in the job runner logs, followed by job‑specific messages, and `send_email` logs for the onboarding emails or alerts it triggers. The `Job` records move from ready to taken to done in the DB, and any related welcome or tip messages appear in the user’s inbox. Combined with the continuous `send email to …, subject '…'` logs from `send_email` and the bounce or complaint handling logs in `email_handler`, this behavior tells me that internal schedulers and email handling components are working across normal deliveries, replies and edge cases. I clean up any temporary test users by directly removing the associated records: first updating the user's `default_mailbox_id` to `NULL`, then deleting from the `mailbox` table where `user_id` matches, and finally deleting from the `users` table where the email matches the test account. I verify cleanup is complete by running `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE email = 'testuser@example.com'` and confirming a zero count, along with similar zero-count checks on the `mailbox` and `activation_code` tables for that user.
